description: PasswordsCon talks from BSides Las Vegas 2024.

talks.title: Detecting Credential Abuse
talks.teaser: Explains detection patterns for stolen and forged credentials, covering impossible travel and credential binding violations.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why attackers want credentials. Account compromise can fuel spam, fraud or ransomware, or give an intruder an initial foothold, a path for lateral movement, or a route to privilege escalation. The presenters treat credentials both as proof of identity and as keys to access, and note that stronger authentication and tighter binding to a device make a credential more trustworthy. They stress that good logging comes first, since detections are only as reliable as the data behind them.

The core of the session covers detection patterns at identity providers. Impossible travel flags sign-ins whose implied travel speed is unrealistic, but IP geolocation is noisy because of VPNs and shifting address blocks, so they recommend combining indicators across log sources and weighting each by how portable the credential is. Credential binding checks compare a device, TLS channel, IP range or time window against where a credential was issued, and a failed check is logged as a violation. For forged credentials, a usage event with no matching creation event suggests the credential was minted out of band. Credential sharing and sale are harder to handle because the user may be complicit.

The response section stresses establishing scope, whether the credential still works, and what the attacker did afterward. Investigators should test hypotheses rather than assume intent, and keep the affected user in mind when forcing logouts or reauthentication. Trade-offs include log volume, alert fatigue and the friction that controls add. Detection at the identity provider, layered with controls, is presented as more practical than chasing every possible theft method.

talks.title: Picking a fight with the banks
talks.teaser: Explores how shared accounts and weak access controls in personal banking enable financial abuse, and what would fix them.
talks.summary:
Cecilie Wian, who specialises in abusability, examines how systems can be turned against the people who use them. This talk focuses on personal banking in Norway, where online banking is routine and where, she argues, private customers get fewer protections than businesses do.

The core problem is that account access is all or nothing. Power of attorney and shared accounts give one person full visibility into another's money and transaction history, and the bank sends no notice when access is granted. Private customers cannot see access logs, while even very small businesses can. Paper forms remain valid, and the speaker described how a one-page form with two witnesses, never checked against a signature on file, gave a volunteer full access to an account. Businesses can also set up dual signing and transaction limits, which private accounts usually lack.

The speaker described trying to get attention for these findings. Earlier reports were often dismissed as intended features, so she wrote a reader letter to a major financial newspaper and later took part in a televised debate with a bank director. That led to more coverage and invitations from other institutions. For practitioners, the takeaway is to treat shared finances as a threat model, and to ask banks for approval by two people, access logs, and alerts whenever access changes.

talks.title: Breaking Historical Ciphertexts with Modern Means
talks.teaser: Explains how classical ciphers from centuries past are broken today using frequency analysis and hill climbing.
talks.summary:
Klaus Schmeh and Elonka Dunin open by noting that many thousands of old ciphertexts survive in archives and collections, and that a large number remain unsolved. Historical codebreaking differs from modern cryptanalysis: the algorithm is usually unknown, and the aim is recovering the plaintext rather than a key. The talk starts with monoalphabetic substitution, where frequency analysis is the standard first step, illustrated with a 17th-century alchemical cryptogram and a 19th-century Freemason document.

Short texts defeat frequency analysis, so the presenters turn to hill climbing: a random substitution key is altered, and the change is kept only if a letter-frequency score improves. Simulated annealing helps the search escape local maxima. For transposition ciphers such as turning grilles, scoring relies on letter pairs instead, and a large grille challenge published online was solved within a few hours. The nomenclator section covers codes that mix letters with whole words, and the Zodiac Killer's Z340 cipher, which was solved by a three-person team in 2020 using computers.

The closing section covers unsolved examples including the Voynich manuscript and the CIA's Kryptos part four. The presenters say generative AI has not yet cracked them. In the Q&A they addressed layered encryption, one-time pads and practice resources. The takeaway is that historical codebreaking is an active research area, with hill climbing currently the strongest general method, and many puzzles remain open for anyone who wants to try them.

talks.title: Passwords 101
talks.teaser: Traces password hashing history and shows how a 1,576-password DES crypt dump was cracked with wordlists and rules.
talks.summary:
Jeff Deifik opens with the basics of password storage. He explains how salts stop identical passwords from producing identical hashes, and why unsalted schemes such as Windows LAN Manager and old DES crypt are cheap to attack with precomputed tables. He contrasts these with modern algorithms like bcrypt, whose salts make precomputation impractical.

The core of the talk is a personal project: cracking a dump of 1,576 DES crypt passwords over about five years. He compares John the Ripper and hashcat, noting their different rule syntaxes, and describes how low-quality wordlists had to be cleaned with custom Python utilities alongside sort, uniq and comm. He covers mangling rules, a GPU build chosen for performance per watt, and a group of passwords that used control characters. Those were only found by adding insertion and substitution rules to a large dictionary. The same approach was applied to a leaked set of 1980s BSD Unix password hashes.

He closes with defenses: multi-factor authentication, long random passwords sized to what they protect, and a password manager so every service gets a unique credential, since other services' storage practices cannot be verified. He also suggests undervolting GPUs to cut power use and heat.

talks.title: That's not my name
talks.teaser: Shows how character encoding mistakes garble names, emails and passwords, and why UTF-8 mix-ups keep happening.
talks.summary:
Bård Aase opens with a personal problem: his Norwegian name, which contains a letter outside basic ASCII, keeps arriving mangled in marketing emails, receipts, and greetings from banks and vendors. That sets up a tour of how text is stored as numbers, and why plain text carries no label saying which encoding it uses.

The middle of the talk walks through recurring failure patterns. UTF-8 bytes are often read as Latin-1, Windows code page 1252 or Mac Roman, and text can be re-encoded each time it passes through another system, so one letter turns into two or more characters. He shows how old code pages, HTML's handling of ISO 8859-1, and the Angstrom sign, which many applications silently convert, produce familiar errors. He also covers how one visible character can be built from combining marks in different byte orders, and how the UTF-16 byte order mark can leak into files.

The closing discussion moved to passwords and security. A listener reported a Norwegian bank login that worked from a phone but not from a PC, apparently because of combining characters. Aase also noted that lookalike Unicode characters can make a spoofed domain appear to match a real one. The practical takeaways are to treat text input as untrusted, normalise it consistently, and state the expected encoding explicitly at every system boundary.

talks.title: Combating phone spoofing with STIR/SHAKEN
talks.teaser: Explains how STIR/SHAKEN authenticates caller ID to help curb phone number spoofing.

talks.title: Long Live Short Lived Credentials - Auto-rotating Secrets At Scale
talks.teaser: Explains how to gather scattered secrets into one manager and automate their rotation with open-source tooling.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking how long it takes to rotate every API key and cloud credential, then uses a breach example in which stolen credentials spread across several connected services and forced thousands of keys to be replaced. The speaker cites industry breach reports that name leaked or stolen credentials as a leading root cause, and notes research suggesting machine identities far outnumber human ones in modern environments.

The core advice is to take things one step at a time. Where possible, remove standing credentials altogether, use phishing-resistant MFA for people, and gather every remaining secret into a single secrets manager with encryption and central reporting. Secrets should be prioritized, starting with crown jewels, then legacy secrets, and finally forgotten "zombie" secrets. Discovery relies on scanners such as TruffleHog and Gitleaks, and rotation follows a create, test, swap, and clean-up pattern. The speaker covers cloud-native vaults for single-cloud shops, multi-cloud options, and an open-source workflow that finds exposed secrets and opens pull requests to replace them with vault lookups.

Looking further ahead, the speaker points to short-lived workload identities such as SPIFFE and SPIRE, which issue credentials that expire quickly. In audience questions, legacy systems, databases, and SaaS tools that depend on manual admin consoles were raised as hard to automate, and the speaker suggested business risk should decide how far to go. The main takeaway is to start with one secret at a time.

talks.title: Zero downtime credential rotation
talks.teaser: Shows how to rotate service credentials with no redeployments or downtime, using three patterns and lessons from a real system.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a familiar problem: teams avoid changing service credentials because they fear breaking systems or causing costly outages. The speaker argues that credentials will eventually leak, so they should be rotated quickly and routinely, and that practicing rotation reveals hidden weaknesses in a system before an incident does.

He separates symmetric credentials, such as passwords and API keys, from derived, short-lived ones like JSON web tokens and certificates. He contrasts push models, where secrets are injected at deploy time, with pull models, where applications re-read secrets as needed. Three rotation approaches are presented: overlapping blue and green credentials, fail-and-retry against the secret manager, and refreshing derived credentials after a fraction of their lifetime has passed. He then describes problems his team hit while rolling this out, including credentials shared across unrelated clients, retry loops without delay that overwhelmed their own services, leaked threads from failed connections, service accounts that could be locked out by anyone who knew the username, and commercial software that needed restarts to pick up new secrets.

The takeaways are to split credentials along logical boundaries, add jitter and backoff, make client libraries tunable with callbacks and file watches, log credential failures at warning level or above, and use layered alerts on both application errors and secret manager access. He also urges teams to rotate during business hours and to publish dashboards so other groups can see recent changes.

talks.title: CVE Hunting: Wi-Fi Routers, OSINT & 'The Tyranny of the Default'
talks.teaser: Walks through hunting CVEs in Wi-Fi routers using open-source research and the risks of default configurations.

talks.title: Practical Perimeter-less authentication solutions for Startups using AWS native solutions
talks.teaser: Shows how small companies can drop VPN dependence using AWS Systems Manager and Verified Access under zero trust principles.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a security consultant who works with small and medium businesses, argues that VPN-based perimeters fall short for cloud-hosted companies. Long-lived credentials such as SSH keys, user passwords and VPN configs create many entry points, and firms with tight budgets often lack the resources for a full zero trust rollout. The talk frames zero trust as continuous authentication and authorization driven by device, network, identity and permission signals.

Demos cover AWS Systems Manager working with IAM Identity Center. Engineers sign in with federated credentials and MFA, receive temporary credentials, and reach instances over SSM sessions, port forwarding to an internal web server, and a tunnel to a private MySQL database that closes when the session ends. For internal web apps, the talk then shows AWS Verified Access, which applies a policy check without a VPN. Its per-endpoint, per-hour pricing is presented as the main obstacle for small teams, and grouping apps behind a load balancer or tearing endpoints down outside working hours are offered as ways to reduce spend.

The closing advice is that zero trust controls matter even for small companies, that SSM is worth exploring because it adds little or no cost, and that Verified Access suits web tools such as a dev server or an internal Jenkins instance rather than database access. The speaker's final point is that strong controls depend more on intent than on money.

talks.title: We removed passwords, now what?
talks.teaser: Explores how account recovery and identity verification must change once an organization removes passwords in favor of passkeys.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the growth of passkeys, including security keys, platform authenticators and synced passkeys, and the trade-offs of each. Passwordless sign-in creates a problem for account recovery, because the usual fallbacks such as SMS codes, email, one-time passwords and support calls each have weaknesses, and support calls can be abused through social engineering. The speaker presents identity verification as the replacement check and gives examples where it went wrong: a hiring case where the person who started work was not the person who was interviewed, a government verification flow that relied on scripted video reads, and a ride-sharing profile that showed verification passed despite an obvious problem.

The middle of the talk covers the difficulties of identity verification itself. Storing IDs, selfies and videos creates personal data risk, purchased selfies and deepfakes can defeat checks, recorded video can expose a person's surroundings, and face matching that never tested negative cases accepted clearly different faces. A sample recovery flow chains a username, an SMS code, a location check, an ID scan, facial recognition and a manager review. The talk also notes user friction, such as a bank that repeated verification after a phone change.

The closing recommendations are to add identity verification to account recovery, use an established vendor because of legal and regulatory obligations, test negative cases and not only the successful path, and move toward passwordless sign-in where possible. The Q&A covered liveness detection against deepfakes and the trade-off between convenience and security in choosing how passkeys are stored.

talks.title: Cloud Attack: Dissecting Attack Paths with Graph-Mode
talks.teaser: Walks through cloud identity misconfigurations and shows how graph-mode tooling maps privilege escalation paths.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with definitions of threat, high value target and attack path, and argues that in cloud environments almost any identity can become a high value target. A single over-permissioned user, group or role can expose many resources, so the speaker frames identity and access management as the central control point. The explanation of AWS policies covers their statements, effects and action lists, and shows why broad read-only or wildcard grants can still help an attacker enumerate accounts and users.

The middle section works through a lab scenario in which a managed-looking policy with one permission-management action, granted on all resources and set as the default version, lets an attacker create a new policy version and widen their access, reaching organization-level control. The speaker then demonstrates an open-source graph tool built on Neo4j that queries principals, policies and statements to find such escalation paths, along with a free community edition of a commercial identity platform that visualizes attack paths and suggests remediation as infrastructure code. The question-and-answer segment covers how attack modules map specific actions to identities, and how similar reasoning could extend to other cloud platforms, CI/CD systems and directory synchronization accounts.

The takeaway for practitioners is to review cloud permissions action by action rather than by policy name, since AWS offers thousands of actions and default policy versions can quietly change what a grant allows. Graph-based views of identities and their relationships can surface chained privileges before an attacker finds them.

talks.title: All your badge are belong to me
talks.teaser: Shows how RFID access badges fail through default keys, cloning and replay attacks, drawn from physical penetration tests.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at radio-frequency identification badges used in building access control, a technology whose weaknesses have been documented for years yet still appear in new installations. The speaker, a penetration tester, explains how readers, controllers and management servers fit together, and why a compromise of one badge or of the management software can expose the whole system.

The core of the talk is a set of field findings. Older MIFARE Classic cards were protected by factory-default keys that were reused across many customers, so one key list could dump cards from unrelated buildings. Some systems rely only on the card's unique ID, which is easy to read and copy. Guest and PIN handling was often weak, management interfaces were found exposed to the internet with default credentials, and the link between reader and controller was shown to be open to replay. Physical tests included a temporary office where found badges were cloned, and a master card kept in a simple key box that anyone could open.

The closing sections turn to why insecure systems keep being bought. Procurement that focuses on price, and installers who lack protocol knowledge, both play a part, and upgrading often means replacing readers, controllers and servers. The practical takeaways are to never use default keys, avoid ID-only credentials, write security requirements into tenders, and prefer newer encrypted card types.
